newsitem.title: UK: OECD reliance on Middle East oil falling - IEA.
newsitem.headline: OECD reliance on Middle East oil falling - IEA.

text.p: The world's leading industrial nations are relying less on crude oil imports from the Middle East as their own supplies increase, the International Energy Agency (IEA) said on Thursday.
"Although crude imports into OECD countries increased by 3.4 percent in 1996, imports from the Middle East declined by 1.6 percent," the IEA said.
"Imports from OECD countries, mainly Norway and Mexico, rose by 7.9 percent, while imports from non-OECD countries showed an increase of only 1.7 percent," the Paris-based agency said.

The eleven members of the Organisation of Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC) saw their imports to the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) area rise by only 0.9 percent last year.
OPEC giant Saudi Arabia remained the biggest single supplier to OECD members, although at a declining rate, accounting for 16.5 percent of total imports down from 17.4 percent in 1995.
The IEA said the average crude oil import price for its members rose to $20.52 a barrel in 1996 from $17.19 a barrel the previous year.
Crude oil production in OECD countries increased by 3.7 percent, faster than the world average of 2.8 percent largely because of sharp gains in Norway and Mexico.
OECD demand growth -- at 2.8 percent -- lagged increased supply but was substantially higher than the 0.4 percent reported in 1995, the IEA said.
Unlike crude oil, product imports from outside the OECD grew much faster (14 percent) than from within the OECD.
The former Soviet Union's share of product imports increased by 34.5 percent, the IEA said.
World oil demand in 1995, the last year for which the IEA has complete information, grew by 1.8 percent, mainly due to fast growth in demand for gas oil, diesel, Liquified Petroleum Gas and naphtha.
